doc.title: Ira Gitler interviewed by Michael Woods, New York City, New York, November 16, 1995

title: Interviewing John Coltrane at the Park Central
summary: Gitler describes his Down Beat article on Coltrane, their talk in the hotel, and Coltrane's seriousness and spirituality.

story.theme_name: Playing with Coltrane and the avant-garde

blocks.x: I want to ask you about another major figure that I don’t think we’ve really talked about in depth in any of our interviews so far. And I want to talk about it culturally and spiritually because he had those aspects to his character. Tell us about Coltrane.

Well Coltrane was a serious man. I don’t say he didn’t laugh and didn’t have his own sense of humor, I really didn’t see it personally although I spent some time with him, in fact I heard him a lot. But you know he wasn’t a great conversationalist. Probably if I’d gotten to know him a little better. But I did interview him for a Down Beat article. I wrote the first article about him in a major publication or in any publication I think of any length. And at that time he was between apartments and he was staying at the Park Central Hotel, which later became the Park Sheraton and I think it’s the Park Central again, I can’t keep up with it. Like WHN and WMGM in New York. And so I went up to his room, and you know it was a time when I was working with Prestige as a writer. I wasn’t there every day anymore, but I had been there in the period when he came with

Miles and then became a recording leader in his own right there. And we hung out and talked, and he was very warm and very serious and you know I think a man, at that time, very aware that some people were misinterpreting him. He had been called an “angry young tenor” or something in Down Beat and he said, “I’m only angry at myself when I don’t make what I’m trying to do.” But he was a very spiritual person, there’s no doubt about that. You got that from him. And he battled a lot of demons, and came through it, but it took its toll. And I think about Trane, I think a lot of people talk about his great spirituality in his later work, you know when he really became very pointed towards the spiritual. But he always had it, even when he wasn’t playing “A Love Supreme” or post that, and I think everything he played when it was a ballad it was a very spiritual feeling.
